title: The road the sea owns twice a day
text: {{1}} day, the tide reclaims the causeway that links Mont Saint-Michel to the French coast {{2}} a regularity that has governed the island for thirteen centuries. The bay is famous for tides that race in faster than a galloping horse, and the medieval abbey, {{3}} spire crowns the rock, has watched pilgrims misjudge them for just as long. {{4}} the causeway lies under the sea, the visit must follow the tide tables rather than the clock. Access {{5}} once on foot at low tide, across shining sand that sucked at boots; a bridge built in 2014 now lets the water flow beneath the road, {{6}} means the mount is an island again at every high tide. The rescue boat remains moored nearby, {{7}} it has been for generations, and every year the sea adds a few more abandoned cars to its collection. The mount itself has never minded: it has simply waited {{8}} the water twice a day, as it always has.

gaps.explanation: 'Whose' links the abbey to its spire.

gaps.explanation: Time clause governing the visit: when.

gaps.explanation: Sentential relative after the comma: which means.
